title: Good news to the poor (Isaiah 61:1–3)
hookLine: beauty for ashes: the passage Jesus read in Nazareth

cards: A small-town synagogue on the Sabbath. Everyone knows everyone. Joseph's son is back from teaching around Galilee.

He stands up to read, and the attendant hands him a scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He unrolls it, finds the place he wants, and reads a few lines aloud. Then he rolls it up, hands it back, and sits down.
The room goes quiet. Luke's Gospel says every eye in the place was fixed on him. This is his hometown, Nazareth.

teach.h: ANOINTED: GOOD TIDINGS TO THE POOR.
teach.b: Isaiah sixty-one begins, in the King James Bible: "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound."
The Hebrew word behind meek also means the poor, the bowed down, the ones with no power. And anointed shares a root with the word messiah.
Then verse three: "to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness."

teach.h: PE'ER TACHAT EFER: A CROWN FOR ASHES.
teach.b: In Hebrew, beauty for ashes is a little rhyme, pe'er tachat efer. Ashes were what mourners put on their heads. Pe'er was a festive headdress, a garland.
The head that wore ashes now wears a crown. Back to Nazareth.

teach.h: THIS DAY IS THIS SCRIPTURE FULFILLED.
teach.b: Jesus reads from this passage, Luke tells us, then sits down and says: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears."
Luke sets it at the start of Jesus' public work, and Christians often read it as his program: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed.

Isaiah's sentence goes on: to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God. Luke has Jesus stop after the year of the Lord's favor, rolling up the scroll mid-sentence.
Some Christian readers make much of that pause: in their reading, he came announcing favor first.

how: Churches often read Isaiah 61 and Luke 4 together, and Christians often describe the passage as Jesus's mission statement; it is read at ordinations and in services focused on the poor, the sick and the imprisoned.

o: a prophet's robe worn to read in the synagogue
a festive garland worn in place of mourning ashes
the oil poured on a king's head at his crowning

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.

s: in Luke, Jesus reads Isaiah's sentence to the end
he stops after the acceptable year of the Lord, before the day of vengeance.
beauty for ashes is a rhyme in Hebrew
pe'er tachat efer: a garland instead of ashes.
the meek, in Isaiah 61, means the shy
the Hebrew means the poor and bowed down, the ones with no power.

games.q: you're in the synagogue at Nazareth. the hometown teacher has just read Isaiah and sat down. what does he say?
o: this will happen someday, far in the future.
this day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.
let us discuss what the prophet meant.
games.why: "this day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." Luke places it at the start of Jesus' public work.

practice: Bring to mind someone wearing ashes right now, in their own way, a fresh loss, a divorce, a diagnosis, the anniversary of a death, and picture them as they are, without hurrying them toward the garland; in the book of Job, a mourner sits in the ashes, and his friends sit down with him in silence.
Then think of one small thing that could be a bit of oil of gladness for them: a meal, a note, a visit, a memory shared. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Pe'er. The festive garland Isaiah promises in place of ashes, worn by the brokenhearted and the captives: the passage Jesus read aloud in Nazareth.

orig.note: Hebrew: a garland instead of ashes. the two nouns share the same letters.

carryVoice: Your line: beauty for ashes. A crown where the ashes used to be. See you tomorrow.
